entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An elected official, especially a president, who is near the end of a term and has little real power, often because a successor has already been chosen.
entries.usage: Very common in American political news, also as an adjective: *a lame-duck president*, *the lame-duck session* of Congress between the November election and January. It describes a situation rather than insulting the person. In British English it can also mean a struggling company or person that needs help.
examples: After his party lost the election, the governor was **a lame duck** for his last two months in office.
Congress rushed to pass the bill during the **lame-duck** session in December.
As soon as she announced she wouldn't run again, the mayor became **a lame duck**, and the council stopped listening to her.

drill.sentence: Once the trustees picked her successor, the university president was {{a lame duck}} for the rest of the school year.
drill.hint: a leader with little power at the end of her time in the job (a bird image)

entries.related: *outgoing* — leaving office soon, neutral; *a caretaker government* — a temporary government until a new one is formed; *a spent force* — someone who has lost their power.
entries.origin: First used on the London Stock Exchange in the 18th century for a trader who could not pay his debts.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of a joke, an explanation or a hint: to be too difficult or too subtle for someone to understand.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often about jokes, hints and technical talk: *The joke went right over his head.* *Right* or *completely* often comes before *over*. The same phrase also means contacting someone's boss to get a decision, so context matters.
examples: I made a joke about Shakespeare, but it **went right over the kids' heads**.
Most of the talk on quantum computing **went over my head**, but the slides were beautiful.
I kept hinting that I wanted a dog for my birthday, but it **went completely over his head**.

drill.sentence: The cartoon is full of jokes for parents that {{go right over kids' heads}}.
drill.hint: pass above children's understanding (not *fly …*)

entries.related: *be lost on someone* — not be understood or appreciated by them; *over my head* — too difficult for me; *go over someone's head* (second sense) — contact their boss directly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An experience or a fact that surprises you and shows you something important that you did not know or understand before.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and reviews, usually with *real*, *quite* or *a bit of*: *The trip was a real eye-opener.* It is usually about learning how things really are, often something unpleasant. The adjective is *eye-opening*: *an eye-opening documentary*.
examples: Volunteering at the food bank was **an eye-opener**; I had no idea how many families in our town go hungry.
Working a retail job over the holidays was **a real eye-opener** about how rude people can be.
Reading other people's training code was **an eye-opener**: almost nobody set their random seeds.

drill.sentence: Living in Tokyo for a year was {{an eye-opener}}; I realized how many American habits I'd taken for granted.
drill.hint: an experience that showed me surprising things (not *a revelation*)

entries.related: *a revelation* — a surprising discovery, more formal; *a wake-up call* — a warning that makes you change your behavior; *open someone's eyes to* — make them aware of.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid looking foolish or losing other people's respect, especially after a mistake or a defeat.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and social life, often about a compromise that lets someone avoid public humiliation: *a way to save face*, *let someone save face*. The opposite is *lose face*. The adjective is *face-saving*: *a face-saving deal*.
examples: He knew he was wrong, but he kept arguing just to **save face** in front of his friends.
The deal let both governments **save face** and claim a victory at home.
Instead of admitting she'd been fired, she told everyone she had quit to **save face**.

drill.sentence: My uncle got us lost on the drive but insisted he was taking a 'scenic route' to {{save face}}.
drill.hint: avoid looking foolish (not *… pride*)

entries.related: *lose face* — the opposite, lose respect in public; *swallow your pride* — accept a humbling situation; *a face-saving gesture* — an action that helps someone avoid embarrassment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make someone stay alert and ready to react, usually because things keep changing or are hard to predict.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, often with a positive or humorous tone: small children, surprise quizzes and demanding bosses *keep you on your toes*. The pronouns change together: *keep us on our toes*, *keep them on their toes*. *Be on your toes* simply means to be alert.
examples: Our chemistry teacher gave surprise quizzes to **keep us on our toes**.
Twin toddlers **keep you on your toes**; the moment you sit down, one of them is climbing something.
The new coach changes the lineup every week to **keep the players on their toes**.

drill.sentence: My grandmother likes to change the rules of Monopoly halfway through the game, just to {{keep us on our toes}}.
drill.hint: make us stay alert (not *… guessing*)

entries.related: *keep someone guessing* — keep them unsure about what you will do; *on the ball* — alert and quick; *catch someone off guard* — surprise someone who isn't ready.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A lasting feeling of resentment, or a need to prove yourself, usually because you feel you were treated unfairly in the past.
entries.usage: Used about people who are quick to take offense or are driven to prove others wrong. The pattern is *have a chip on your shoulder about* something. It is usually critical, but in sports talk it can be positive motivation: *He plays with a chip on his shoulder.*
entries.pattern: have a chip on your shoulder (about something)
examples: He's had **a chip on his shoulder** about his height since high school.
The quarterback was drafted late, and he plays every game with **a chip on his shoulder**.
She has **a chip on her shoulder** about not finishing college, so she hears every comment as criticism.

drill.sentence: My cousin grew up poor in a rich town, and he still has {{a chip on his shoulder}} about it.
drill.hint: a lasting resentment about being treated unfairly (not *a grudge*)

entries.related: *hold a grudge* — stay angry at a specific person; *have something to prove* — feel you must show your ability; *touchy* — easily offended.
entries.origin: Often traced to 19th-century America, where a boy looking for a fight would put a wood chip on his shoulder and dare others to knock it off.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have an advantage or more control than someone else in a situation, a contest or a negotiation.
entries.usage: Common in sports, politics, business and relationships. Typical verbs are *have*, *gain*, *get* and *give someone* the upper hand, often followed by *over* or *in*: *gain the upper hand over your rivals*. It is neutral and describes the balance of power.
examples: Once the other team's best player fouled out, we **had the upper hand**.
In a seller's market, homeowners **have the upper hand** in negotiations.
My little sister always **has the upper hand** in arguments because she remembers everything I've ever said.

drill.sentence: In chess, controlling the center early usually gives you {{the upper hand}}.
drill.hint: more control than your opponent (a body-part image)

entries.related: *have the edge* — have a small advantage; *in the driver's seat* — in control; *hold all the cards* — have every advantage.

entries.term: can't put your finger on something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be unable to identify exactly what is wrong, different or strange about something, although you can sense it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, usually as *I can't put my finger on it* or *I can't quite put my finger on what's wrong*. It is almost always negative, and *quite* is a common addition. The object is usually *it* or a *what* clause.
examples: Something about the new guy bothers me, but I **can't put my finger on it**.
The soup tastes different, but I **can't quite put my finger on** what's changed.
Her doctors knew something was wrong but **couldn't put their finger on** the cause for months.

drill.sentence: You look different today. New glasses? A haircut? I {{can't put my finger on it}}.
drill.hint: am unable to say exactly what it is (a hand image)

entries.related: *pinpoint* — identify exactly, more formal; *something is off* — something feels wrong; *a nagging feeling* — a feeling that won't go away.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do hard, practical or unpleasant work yourself instead of leaving it to others.
entries.usage: Common at work and in conversation, usually as praise for someone senior who still does practical work: *a manager who isn't afraid to get her hands dirty*. It can also mean getting involved in something dishonest, so context matters. The pronoun changes: *get his / their hands dirty*.
examples: Our CEO isn't afraid to **get her hands dirty**; she worked the warehouse floor during the holiday rush.
If you want a vegetable garden like this one, you have to **get your hands dirty**.
The best way to learn statistics is to **get your hands dirty** with real, messy data.

drill.sentence: My dad hired a contractor, but he still {{got his hands dirty}} and helped tear out the old kitchen himself.
drill.hint: did the hard physical work himself (not *pitched in*)

entries.related: *roll up your sleeves* — get ready to work hard; *pitch in* — help with a shared task; *hands-on* — involved in practical work.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be deeply affected by criticism or advice: to feel hurt by it, or to take it seriously and act on it.
entries.usage: It has two sides: *Don't take it to heart* means don't be upset, while *I took your advice to heart* means I followed it seriously. It is used with criticism, comments, advice and lessons. The object usually comes before *to heart*: *take his words to heart*.
examples: The coach said I was lazy on defense, and I **took it to heart**; I trained twice as hard all summer.
Don't **take it to heart**; Grandpa is grumpy with everyone.
The company **took the criticism to heart** and redesigned the app from scratch.

drill.sentence: She's very sensitive, so if you criticize her cooking, she'll {{take it to heart}} and sulk for days.
drill.hint: be deeply hurt by it (not *… personally* or *… hard*)

entries.related: *take something personally* — feel that criticism is an attack on you; *take something on board* — accept and use advice, more British; *shrug something off* — the opposite, not be affected.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A plan, a promise or a hope that is very unlikely ever to happen.
entries.usage: Used critically in politics, business and conversation about unrealistic plans and promises. It works as a noun (*That plan is pie in the sky*) and, with hyphens, before a noun (*a pie-in-the-sky idea*). It is dismissive, so saying it about someone's idea to their face can sound rude.
examples: A four-day workweek at my company is **pie in the sky**; my boss won't even let us work from home on Fridays.
My plan to retire at forty turned out to be **pie in the sky**.
Investors laughed at the startup's **pie-in-the-sky** forecast of a billion users in two years.

drill.sentence: The mayor's promise to end traffic jams by next summer is {{pie in the sky}}.
drill.hint: an unrealistic hope (a food image)

entries.related: *a pipe dream* — a hope that will never come true; *wishful thinking* — believing something because you want it to be true; *castles in the air* — impossible plans, more literary.
entries.origin: From Joe Hill's 1911 protest song *The Preacher and the Slave*, which mocked the promise of a reward in heaven.

entries.term: too many cooks in the kitchen
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which too many people are involved in a task or a decision, so the work becomes confused or worse.
entries.usage: A mild complaint, common in American offices and families. It often follows *there are*: *There are too many cooks in the kitchen on this project.* The older proverb is *too many cooks spoil the broth*.
examples: Five people edited the wedding speech, and it got worse each time: **too many cooks in the kitchen**.
The project stalled because there were **too many cooks in the kitchen** and nobody could make a final decision.
The city's response to the flood was slow; with three agencies in charge, there were **too many cooks in the kitchen**.

drill.sentence: Planning my sister's baby shower with eight aunts was a disaster; there were {{too many cooks in the kitchen}}.
drill.hint: so much help that things went wrong (a restaurant image)

entries.related: *too many cooks spoil the broth* — the full proverb; *design by committee* — a poor result from too many decision-makers; *herding cats* — organizing people who won't cooperate.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To delay an event or a decision on purpose, so that you have more time to prepare or to find a solution.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and everyday life: *buy some time*, *buy yourself time*, *buy time for* someone. It often implies a temporary fix, not a real solution: *The loan just buys us time.* *Stall for time* is similar but sounds more negative.
examples: I asked a clarifying question just to **buy time** while I thought of an answer.
The extra loan won't save the company, but it will **buy us some time**.
Doctors gave her medication to **buy time** until a donor heart became available.

drill.sentence: When Mom asked who broke the vase, my little brother pretended to sneeze to {{buy some time}}.
drill.hint: gain a few extra seconds (not *stall*)

entries.related: *stall for time* — delay on purpose, often dishonestly; *play for time* — similar, more British; *kick the can down the road* — delay a problem instead of solving it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In a better position than others, usually because you prepared early or acted before them.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school and in personal finance: *If you start saving at 25, you're ahead of the game.* Typical verbs are *be*, *get* and *stay*. It is positive and is about early preparation; *ahead of the curve* is more about adopting new trends early.
examples: If you already speak some Spanish before you move to Mexico, you're **ahead of the game**.
Starting your holiday shopping in October puts you way **ahead of the game**.
The company stayed **ahead of the game** by investing in electric trucks before its rivals.

drill.sentence: I finished my taxes in February, so for once I'm {{ahead of the game}}.
drill.hint: in a better position than usual (not *… schedule*)

entries.related: *ahead of the curve* — early to adopt new trends; *get a head start* — start before others; *behind the eight ball* — the opposite, in a difficult position, American.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To remain good, useful or popular for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, journalism and conversation about books, music, buildings, ideas and products. It is positive, and it often appears in questions or with *will*: *Will this design stand the test of time?* *Withstand the test of time* is a slightly more formal variant.
examples: The Beatles' songs have **stood the test of time**; my kids know every word.
Cheap furniture rarely **stands the test of time**, so we saved up for a good table.
Einstein's theory of relativity has **stood the test of time** for more than a century.

drill.sentence: My grandmother's cast-iron skillet is over seventy years old, and it has really {{stood the test of time}}.
drill.hint: remained good after many years (not *held up*)

entries.related: *timeless* — never going out of style; *hold up* — remain good when tested or over time; *a flash in the pan* — the opposite, a short-lived success.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Immediately and without any hesitation, because you are completely sure.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, usually with *would* to show eagerness: *I'd do it again in a heartbeat.* It is about willingness and decisions more than physical speed. It is informal and warm, so it fits personal talk but not formal writing.
examples: If I could retire tomorrow, I'd do it **in a heartbeat**.
She'd move back to Chicago **in a heartbeat** if she found a job there.
People ask if I'd marry him again after all these years. **In a heartbeat**.

drill.sentence: If my favorite band asked me to join their tour, I'd say yes {{in a heartbeat}}.
drill.hint: instantly, with no doubt at all (a body image)

entries.related: *without a second thought* — without hesitating; *in a flash* — very quickly; *in a New York minute* — very quickly, American.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: From the very beginning of something.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and informal writing, often when someone says a problem or a feeling was there from the start: *I knew from the get-go that it wouldn't work.* In formal writing, use *from the outset* or *from the start*. It is written with a hyphen.
examples: I liked my roommate **from the get-go**; we had the same weird sense of humor.
The project had problems **from the get-go**, starting with a budget that was far too small.
Fans were skeptical of the trade **from the get-go**, and the season proved them right.

drill.sentence: My parents never liked my ex; they said {{from the get-go}} that he wasn't right for me.
drill.hint: right at the beginning (informal; not *start* or *day one*)

entries.related: *from day one* — from the first day; *from the outset* — more formal; *from scratch* — starting with nothing, not from the beginning of a period.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Bad things tend to happen together: when one problem comes, several others often follow at the same time.
entries.usage: A common American saying, said with a sigh or with humor after several problems arrive at once. It usually stands alone as a comment, after the speaker lists the problems. The British version is *it never rains but it pours*.
examples: First the dishwasher broke, then the basement flooded; **when it rains, it pours**.
I lost my job, and a week later my landlord raised the rent. **When it rains, it pours**.
**When it rains, it pours**: the team lost its starting quarterback and its best receiver in the same game.

drill.sentence: I got a flat tire on the way to my job interview, and then I spilled coffee all over my shirt. Well, {{when it rains, it pours}}.
drill.hint: bad things come all at once (a weather saying)

entries.related: *it never rains but it pours* — the British version; *a double whammy* — two bad things at once; *one thing after another* — a plain complaint about many problems.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get organized and start behaving in a more responsible or effective way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually as criticism or a warning to someone who is disorganized or lazy: *You need to get your act together.* Said directly to someone, it is blunt, but it is also used about yourself or about institutions. The pronoun changes: *get his / its act together*.
examples: If you don't **get your act together**, you're going to fail this class.
After his second warning at work, he finally **got his act together** and started showing up on time.
The city needs to **get its act together**; the trash hasn't been picked up in two weeks.

drill.sentence: I've been eating junk and skipping the gym for months; it's time I {{got my act together}}.
drill.hint: got organized and responsible (a theater word)

entries.related: *shape up* — improve your behavior; *pull yourself together* — control your emotions; *get it together* — same, more casual.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To cause an emotional reaction in people, usually because something feels familiar or true to their own experience.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, journalism and conversation about books, songs, speeches and ideas. The people follow *with*: *The song struck a chord with young voters.* *Strike a nerve* is different: it means touching a sensitive topic that upsets people.
examples: Her speech about caring for aging parents **struck a chord** with many people in the audience.
The ad **struck a chord** with millennials who can't afford to buy a home.
Something about the old photo **struck a chord**; it reminded me of my grandfather's farm.

drill.sentence: The novel about a lonely immigrant teenager {{struck a chord}} with readers all over the world.
drill.hint: moved people because it felt true (a music image; not *resonated*)

entries.related: *resonate with* — feel meaningful to someone; *strike a nerve* — touch a sensitive, upsetting topic; *hit home* — make someone realize something, often painfully.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of words, promises or apologies: to sound insincere or unconvincing, usually because they do not match the facts or the speaker's actions.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, politics and serious conversation, usually about apologies, promises, praise and excuses. The subject is the words, not the speaker: *His apology rang hollow.* The listener often follows *to* or *for*: *The promises rang hollow to voters.*
examples: His apology **rang hollow** because he made the same joke again the next day.
The company's talk about valuing its workers **rings hollow** after another round of layoffs.
Promises to fix the potholes **ring hollow** to residents who have heard them every election.

drill.sentence: My brother said he was sorry for missing my birthday again, but the words {{rang hollow}}.
drill.hint: sounded insincere (a bell image)

entries.related: *ring true* — the opposite, seem believable; *lip service* — support in words but not in action; *empty promises* — promises that won't be kept.

entries.term: throw a wrench in the works
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something that causes a plan or a process to fail or be delayed.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and news; the British version is *put a spanner in the works*. The subject is often an event, not a person: *The storm threw a wrench in the works.* Variants include *throw a (monkey) wrench into* something and *throw a wrench in our plans*.
examples: We were ready to close on the house, but a problem with the inspection **threw a wrench in the works**.
The snowstorm **threw a wrench in the works** for thousands of holiday travelers.
My sister **threw a wrench in the works** by announcing she was bringing four extra guests.

drill.sentence: We had the whole surprise party planned until Dad came home early and {{threw a wrench in the works}}.
drill.hint: messed up the plan (a tool image)

entries.related: *put a spanner in the works* — the British version; *upset the apple cart* — spoil a plan or a stable situation; *derail* — make a plan fail.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To speak or act quickly and directly, without careful thought or preparation.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and political commentary. It can be critical (careless, reckless) or admiring (honest, decisive), depending on the speaker. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *a shoot-from-the-hip style*.
examples: My boss tends to **shoot from the hip** in emails and then spends the next day apologizing.
I'm not going to **shoot from the hip** on this; give me a day to look at the numbers.
Fans love the coach's **shoot-from-the-hip** honesty, even when it gets him fined by the league.

drill.sentence: My dad tends to {{shoot from the hip}} when he gives advice, so take what he says with a grain of salt.
drill.hint: speak quickly without thinking (a gunfighter image)

entries.related: *think on your feet* — react quickly and well, positive; *off the cuff* — without preparation; *speak your mind* — say what you think honestly.
entries.origin: From firing a gun from hip level without raising it to aim, as gunfighters do in Westerns.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The most extreme action available, used only as a last resort because its effects are drastic.
entries.usage: Common in American political news, where it often means changing Senate rules by a simple majority so that a filibuster cannot block certain votes. In everyday speech it is often humorous: deleting a group chat or calling someone's mother. Typical verbs are *use*, *go for*, *invoke* and *threaten*.
examples: If the landlord doesn't fix the heat by Friday, we'll go for **the nuclear option** and call the city.
Senate leaders threatened to use **the nuclear option** to end filibusters on judicial nominees.
Deleting the whole group chat was **the nuclear option**, but the arguments had gone on for weeks.

drill.sentence: My sister and I couldn't agree on a movie, so Mom went with {{the nuclear option}}: no TV for the whole weekend.
drill.hint: the most drastic step (a bomb image)

entries.related: *a last resort* — what you do when everything else has failed; *pull the plug* — stop something completely; *scorched earth* — destroying everything, even at great cost.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Without any special conditions, obligations or hidden costs.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, ads and business, usually after an offer: *a free trial, no strings attached*. Before a noun it takes hyphens: *a no-strings-attached loan*. It is also used about casual relationships without commitment.
examples: My uncle lent me five thousand dollars to start the business, **no strings attached**.
The foundation gives schools money with **no strings attached**, so teachers can spend it however they want.
They agreed to keep things casual, with **no strings attached**.

drill.sentence: The gym is offering a free one-month membership, {{no strings attached}}.
drill.hint: without any hidden conditions (not *no commitment*)

entries.related: *with strings attached* — the opposite, with conditions; *no catch* — no hidden problem; *no questions asked* — without asking for reasons or details.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To challenge someone to actually do what they are threatening, because you believe they are not serious.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business, negotiation and family life: *She threatened to quit, so her boss called her bluff.* The pattern is *call someone's bluff* or *call the bluff of* someone. Afterward the other person must either act or back down.
examples: My son threatened to run away, so I **called his bluff** and offered to help him pack.
The union said it would strike, and management decided to **call its bluff**.
If you keep saying you'll quit the band, one day someone will **call your bluff**.

drill.sentence: The other driver kept saying he'd call the police, so I {{called his bluff}} and handed him my phone.
drill.hint: dared him to do what he threatened (a poker image)

entries.related: *bluff* — pretend you will do something or have something; *put up or shut up* — act on your words or stop talking; *back down* — give up a threat or a demand.
entries.origin: From poker, where to *call* means to match a bet and make a bluffing player show their cards.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which people or groups keep blaming each other for a problem instead of trying to solve it.
entries.usage: Common in political news and workplace talk, and almost always critical. The usual verb is *play*: *Both parties are playing the blame game.* It often appears in calls for responsibility: *Let's stop playing the blame game and fix this.*
examples: After the flight was canceled, the airline and the airport started playing **the blame game**.
**The blame game** started just minutes after the bridge collapsed.
My kids play **the blame game** every time something in the house gets broken.

drill.sentence: When the group project fell apart, the four students got caught up in {{the blame game}} instead of trying to save it.
drill.hint: accusing each other instead of fixing things (a rhyming phrase)

entries.related: *finger-pointing* — blaming others, same idea; *pass the buck* — push responsibility onto someone else; *take responsibility* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To use the rules of a system in a clever, often dishonest way to get an advantage the rules were not meant to give.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news about taxes, welfare, rankings, tests and loyalty programs. It is critical, though sometimes with a little admiration for the cleverness. *Game* can take other objects too: *game the rankings*, *game the algorithm*.
examples: Some students **game the system** by taking only easy classes to raise their GPAs.
Some frequent flyers **game the system**, booking cheap trips they don't need just to keep their elite status.
Some websites **game the system** with fake reviews so they rank higher on search engines.

drill.sentence: My brother figured out how to {{game the system}} at the grocery store, stacking coupons until most of his food was free.
drill.hint: use the rules cleverly for an unfair advantage (not *beat …* or *work …*)

entries.related: *beat the system* — succeed despite the rules, often admired; *exploit a loophole* — use a gap in the rules; *work the system* — similar, often about benefits.

entries.term: get something over the finish line
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To complete a project, a deal or a law successfully, especially by pushing through its final, difficult stage.
entries.usage: Common in American business and political talk: *get the bill / deal / project over the finish line*. It stresses the last push needed to finish, so it often comes with *finally*, *help* or *need to*. It is informal and positive, with a slightly corporate tone.
entries.pattern: get + object + over the finish line
examples: We need just one more vote to **get the bill over the finish line**.
A loan from my parents helped us **get the house purchase over the finish line**.
The team worked all weekend to **get the new release over the finish line**.

drill.sentence: After three years of bake sales and car washes, the neighborhood finally got the new playground {{over the finish line}}.
drill.hint: to completion (a race image; not *across …*)

entries.related: *see something through* — continue until it is finished; *seal the deal* — complete an agreement; *the home stretch* — the last part of a long task.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In the hidden internal parts or workings of something, such as a machine, a program or an organization.
entries.usage: Common in tech, business and science talk: *what's going on under the hood*, *look under the hood*. It is informal and is used when explaining how something really works, beyond what users see. The literal meaning is the engine area of a car (*bonnet* in British English).
examples: The new phone looks the same as last year's, but **under the hood** it has a much faster chip.
Before you trust the poll, look **under the hood** at how they chose the people they surveyed.
**Under the hood**, the city's budget is in much worse shape than the headlines suggest.

drill.sentence: The charity looks well run, but {{under the hood}} its finances are a mess.
drill.hint: in the hidden inner workings (a car image)

entries.related: *behind the scenes* — out of public view; *the nuts and bolts* — the basic practical parts; *the inner workings* — plain, more formal.

entries.term: the squeaky wheel gets the grease
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The people who complain the loudest or most often are the ones who get attention or help first.
entries.usage: A common American proverb, used both as practical advice (complain and you'll get results) and as a criticism of unfair systems. It is often shortened: *Be the squeaky wheel*, *He's a squeaky wheel*. *Gets the oil* is a less common variant.
examples: I called the airline every day until they rebooked me; **the squeaky wheel gets the grease**.
In this school district, **the squeaky wheel gets the grease**, so the loudest parents get the best teachers.
My mom always told me that **the squeaky wheel gets the grease**, so I'm not shy about asking for a raise.

drill.sentence: Keep calling the insurance company about your claim; {{the squeaky wheel gets the grease}}.
drill.hint: those who complain most get helped first (a machine proverb)

entries.related: *speak up* — say what you need; *make a fuss* — complain loudly; *the nail that sticks out gets hammered down* — the opposite idea, from a Japanese proverb.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To spend time and effort on something without making any real progress.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, at work and in self-help talk, usually in the progressive: *I feel like I'm spinning my wheels.* It suggests frustration and often a need to change strategy. The possessive matches the subject: *spinning their wheels*.
examples: I've been applying for jobs for months, and I feel like I'm just **spinning my wheels**.
Without a clear plan, the committee spent a year **spinning its wheels**.
I spent two days **spinning my wheels** on a bug before realizing I was editing the wrong file.

drill.sentence: We've been talking about remodeling the kitchen for three years, but we're just {{spinning our wheels}}.
drill.hint: putting in effort but getting nowhere (a stuck-car image)

entries.related: *go around in circles* — keep returning to the same point; *get nowhere* — make no progress; *tread water* — stay in the same place without advancing.
entries.origin: From a car stuck in mud or snow, whose wheels spin without moving it forward.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To create the conditions that make something possible or easier in the future.
entries.usage: Common in news, history, business and speeches, often about pioneers, laws and discoveries: *pave the way for future generations*. It is usually positive, but it can describe bad results too: *pave the way for abuse*. *Pave the way to* + noun is also used: *pave the way to peace*.
examples: The first women admitted to medical school **paved the way for** the thousands who followed.
The new trade deal could **pave the way for** cheaper cars and electronics.
My older brother **paved the way for** me; by the time I was a teenager, my parents had relaxed all their rules.

drill.sentence: Jackie Robinson {{paved the way for}} generations of Black players in Major League Baseball.
drill.hint: made it possible for others later (a road-building image; not *opened the door*)

entries.related: *open the door to* — make something possible; *lay the groundwork* — do the basic early work; *blaze a trail* — be the first to do something new.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of an argument, a fact or a situation: to have both good and bad effects, or to apply equally to both sides.
entries.usage: Common in debates, journalism and conversation, often to point out that an argument can be used against the person making it: *That argument cuts both ways.* The subject is a fact, a rule or an argument, not a person. It is close to *a double-edged sword*, but it is a verb phrase.
examples: Low interest rates **cut both ways**: borrowers save money, but savers earn almost nothing.
Living with your best friend **cuts both ways**: you're never lonely, but you're never alone either.
Being a small team **cuts both ways**; we move fast, but one sick day can stop everything.

drill.sentence: If honesty matters so much to you, that {{cuts both ways}}; you need to be honest with me too.
drill.hint: applies equally to each side (a blade image)

entries.related: *a double-edged sword* — something with both good and bad effects; *go both ways* — apply to both sides, more casual; *what's good for the goose is good for the gander* — the same rule should apply to everyone.

entries.term: throw the baby out with the bathwater
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get rid of something valuable while trying to get rid of something bad that is connected to it.
entries.usage: Common in debates, business and conversation, usually as a warning: *Let's not throw the baby out with the bathwater.* It is used when someone wants to reject a whole plan, system or idea because of one problem. *Throw out the baby with the bathwater* is an equally common word order.
examples: The new curriculum has problems, but scrapping it completely would be **throwing the baby out with the bathwater**.
One bad date isn't a reason to delete every dating app; don't **throw the baby out with the bathwater**.
Critics say the reform **throws the baby out with the bathwater** by closing good schools along with failing ones.

drill.sentence: Yes, the service was slow, but the food was amazing; never going back would be {{throwing the baby out with the bathwater}}.
drill.hint: losing the good part along with the bad (a bath-time image)

entries.related: *cut off your nose to spite your face* — hurt yourself while trying to hurt someone else; *overcorrect* — fix a problem so hard that you create a new one.
entries.origin: From a German proverb, *das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten*, first recorded in 1512.

entries.term: the final nail in the coffin
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The last of a series of events or problems that causes something to fail or end completely.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and business, often about a failing company, career, plan or relationship. Variants are *the last nail in the coffin* and *another nail in the coffin*, which means one more step toward failure. It is followed by *for* or *of*: *the final nail in the coffin for the factory*.
examples: Losing its biggest customer was **the final nail in the coffin** for the struggling factory.
His comments about the fans were **the final nail in the coffin** of his coaching career.
When she forgot my birthday again, that was **the final nail in the coffin** for our friendship.

drill.sentence: Online shopping hurt the mall for years, but the pandemic was the final {{nail in the coffin}}.
drill.hint: the blow that ended it for good (a funeral image)

entries.related: *the last straw* — the final problem that makes someone lose patience; *the death knell* — a sign that something will soon end; *seal someone's fate* — make a bad outcome certain.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a very great effort, often more than seems necessary, to do or achieve something.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, followed by *to* + verb: *go to great lengths to protect their privacy*. It can be admiring, or slightly critical when the effort seems excessive. Variants include *go to extraordinary lengths* and *go to any lengths*.
entries.pattern: go to great lengths to + verb
examples: My parents **went to great lengths** to hide our Christmas presents every year.
The celebrity couple **went to great lengths** to keep their wedding secret.
Some companies **go to great lengths** to avoid paying taxes.

drill.sentence: The family {{went to great lengths}} to find their lost dog, putting up posters in every town within twenty miles.
drill.hint: made a huge effort (a distance image; not *all out*)

entries.related: *go out of your way* — make a special effort, often to help someone; *bend over backwards* — try very hard to help or please; *go the extra mile* — do more than is expected.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something only because you have to, without real effort, interest or feeling.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work, relationships and religion, and usually critical: *The team looked like it was just going through the motions.* It often comes with *just* or *only*. It suggests that the outward actions are right but the commitment is missing.
examples: By the end of the losing season, the players were just **going through the motions**.
Our marriage had become routine; we were **going through the motions** and barely talking.
I've been **going through the motions** at work ever since I decided to quit.

drill.sentence: My son practices piano every day, but he's clearly {{going through the motions}}; he plays without any feeling.
drill.hint: doing it without real effort or interest (not *phoning it in*)

entries.related: *phone it in* — do something with minimal effort; *on autopilot* — acting without thinking; *give it your all* — the opposite, make your full effort.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Two bad things that happen at the same time or one right after the other, making a situation much worse.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, especially about money, health and weather. The patterns are *a double whammy of A and B* and *a double whammy for* someone. *A triple whammy* is used, often humorously, for three.
examples: Farmers faced **a double whammy** this year: a long drought and falling crop prices.
Getting the flu the same week my car broke down was **a double whammy**.
Renters are dealing with **a double whammy** of higher rent and higher food prices.

drill.sentence: The ski resort was hit with {{a double whammy}}: a winter with almost no snow and a highway closure.
drill.hint: two bad blows at once (not *a one-two punch*)

entries.related: *a one-two punch* — two quick blows, from boxing; *add insult to injury* — make a bad situation even worse; *when it rains, it pours* — bad things come together.
entries.origin: Popularized in the 1950s by the comic strip *Li'l Abner*, in which a *whammy* was an evil-eye curse.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A hopeful saying that the third attempt will succeed after two failures.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, said before or after a third try, often with humor: *Well, third time's the charm!* The article *the* is often dropped. British English usually says *third time lucky*.
examples: I failed my driving test twice, but **the third time was the charm**.
Two of my sourdough loaves collapsed, but **third time's the charm**, right?
The team has lost in the finals two years in a row, so fans are hoping **the third time's the charm**.

drill.sentence: We've been turned down for two apartments, but we're applying for another one today. {{Third time's the charm}}!
drill.hint: the next try will finally work (an American saying)

entries.related: *third time lucky* — the British version; *if at first you don't succeed, try, try again* — keep trying after failure; *a long shot* — something unlikely to succeed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To describe a situation honestly and directly, even if the truth is unpleasant.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually as praise: *I like her because she tells it like it is.* Some people also use it to excuse plain rudeness as honesty. *Like* works as a conjunction here, which is normal in informal speech.
examples: My doctor **tells it like it is**: she said I'd need surgery if I didn't lose weight.
I love my hairdresser because she **tells it like it is**: if a cut won't suit me, she says so.
I asked my best friend what she really thought of my ex, and she **told it like it was**.

drill.sentence: Grandpa never sugarcoats anything; he just {{tells it like it is}}.
drill.hint: states the truth bluntly (not *speaks his mind*)

entries.related: *speak your mind* — say what you think; *not mince words* — speak directly, even if it offends; *sugarcoat* — the opposite, make bad news sound better.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say what you think directly and strongly, even if it may upset or offend people.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, often to introduce a strong criticism or a quote. It is almost always negative: *didn't mince words*, *never minces words*, *I won't mince words*. A possessive is optional: *She didn't mince her words.*
examples: The judge **didn't mince words**, calling the defendant's actions 'cruel and cowardly.'
My new boss **never minces words**, so I always know exactly where I stand.
Our mechanic **didn't mince words**; he told us the car wasn't worth fixing.

drill.sentence: When I asked my sister what she thought of my business plan, she {{didn't mince words}}: she called it a disaster.
drill.hint: spoke bluntly (a cooking verb; not *hold back*)

entries.related: *pull no punches* — criticize with full force; *tell it like it is* — describe the truth directly; *beat around the bush* — the opposite, avoid saying something directly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The stage in a process after which you can no longer stop or go back, so you must continue.
entries.usage: Common in news, conversation and storytelling about decisions, relationships, crises and climate change. Typical verbs are *reach*, *pass* and *be past*: *We've passed the point of no return.* It sounds serious and dramatic.
examples: Once we sold our house and quit our jobs, we'd passed **the point of no return**.
Scientists warn that some ice sheets may be close to **the point of no return**.
By the second hour of the argument, their friendship had reached **the point of no return**.

drill.sentence: Once the wedding invitations went out, we were past {{the point of no return}}.
drill.hint: the moment when backing out is no longer possible

entries.related: *cross the Rubicon* — make a decision that cannot be reversed; *burn your bridges* — destroy your chance of going back; *a tipping point* — the moment when a big change becomes unstoppable.
entries.origin: From aviation: the point on a flight after which a plane no longer has enough fuel to return to where it started.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a very large amount of money quickly, usually from an investment or a deal.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and business news, and it can sound admiring or envious. The investment usually follows *on* and the field *in* (*make a killing on stocks*, *in real estate*), and an *-ing* verb also works: *make a killing selling umbrellas*. *Make a fortune* is more neutral and suggests a longer process.
examples: My neighbor **made a killing** in real estate when he sold his condo at the top of the market.
Street vendors **make a killing** selling umbrellas whenever it rains in Manhattan.
Some investors **made a killing** on bitcoin, while others lost their savings.

drill.sentence: The kids set up a lemonade stand on the hottest day of the summer and {{made a killing}}.
drill.hint: earned a lot of money fast (not *a fortune*)

entries.related: *make a fortune* — earn a lot of money, not necessarily fast; *clean up* — win or earn a lot, informal; *strike it rich* — suddenly become rich.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make progress, especially slowly or with difficulty.
entries.usage: Common in news, work and conversation, often with *some*, *little*, *real* or *finally*: *We're finally making some headway.* The area of progress follows *on*, *in*, *with* or *against*. *Headway* is uncountable: no *a* and no plural.
entries.pattern: make (some / little / real) headway (on / in / with / against something)
examples: After weeks of talks, negotiators are finally **making headway** on a ceasefire.
I've been cleaning out the garage all weekend, and I'm finally **making some headway**.
Researchers have **made little headway** against the disease in the past twenty years.

drill.sentence: I've been reading War and Peace since January, and I've barely {{made any headway}}.
drill.hint: moved forward at all (a sailing word; not *progress*)

entries.related: *make progress* — plain; *gain ground* — advance against a rival; *get nowhere* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To gradually gain influence, customers or success in an area that others controlled before.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and sports news: *make inroads into / in a market*, *make inroads with young voters*. It describes slow, partial gains, not full control. It is often modified: *make significant inroads*, *make few inroads*.
entries.pattern: make inroads in / into + area; make inroads with + group
examples: Electric cars are slowly **making inroads** in rural areas where pickup trucks have always ruled.
The streaming service has **made inroads** with older viewers who used to watch only cable.
Our local bakery has **made inroads** against the big chain stores by focusing on fresh bread.

drill.sentence: American football has struggled to {{make inroads}} in Europe, where soccer still dominates.
drill.hint: gain influence little by little (not *gain ground* or *catch on*)

entries.related: *gain ground* — advance against a rival; *get a foothold* — establish a first small position; *break into* — enter a market or a field.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do what you promised or threatened to do.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about promises, threats, pledges and debts: *make good on a promise*. It often suggests that people had doubts: *He finally made good on his promise to visit.* Do not confuse it with *make good* alone, which means to become successful.
entries.pattern: make good on + promise / threat / pledge / debt
examples: The contractor **made good on** his promise to finish the deck before the Fourth of July.
My brother finally **made good on** the five hundred dollars he owed me.
The umpire **made good on** his threat and threw the manager out of the game.

drill.sentence: Dad {{made good on}} his promise to take us to Disney World if we all got straight A's.
drill.hint: actually did what he promised (three words; not *followed through on*)

entries.related: *follow through on* — complete what you started or promised; *keep your word* — do what you promised; *renege on* — the opposite, break a promise, formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try to predict what will happen by interpreting small signs or hints.
entries.usage: Common in political and financial journalism: analysts *read the tea leaves* in a central bank statement or an election poll. It often suggests that the signs are unclear and the prediction uncertain. It can sound slightly ironic, as if the analysis were fortune-telling.
examples: Investors are **reading the tea leaves** in the Fed chair's speech for hints of a rate cut.
Employees have been **reading the tea leaves** ever since the CEO canceled the holiday party.
My mom didn't say much about my new boyfriend, so I spent the whole drive home **reading the tea leaves**.

drill.sentence: The coach won't say whether her star player will start on Sunday, so fans are {{reading the tea leaves}} in every practice photo.
drill.hint: trying to predict from small signs (a fortune-teller image)

entries.related: *read between the lines* — find a hidden meaning in what someone says; *gaze into a crystal ball* — try to predict the future, often ironic; *Kremlinology* — guessing from small signs what a secretive government is doing.
entries.origin: From fortune-telling based on the patterns that tea leaves leave in the bottom of a cup.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The general situation in a place or an organization: who has influence, how things work and what the problems are.
entries.usage: Common in American English at work and in conversation, typically with *get*, *learn* or *find out*: *I spent my first week getting the lay of the land.* British English usually says *the lie of the land*. The literal meaning is the shape and features of an area of land.
examples: I spent my first month at the new job just getting **the lay of the land** before suggesting any changes.
Before we buy a house there, let's spend a weekend in town and get **the lay of the land**.
Ask the receptionist; she knows **the lay of the land** better than anyone in the building.

drill.sentence: On the first day of college, my roommate and I walked around campus to get {{the lay of the land}}.
drill.hint: a general sense of the place and how it works (not *our bearings*)

entries.related: *the lie of the land* — the British version; *get your bearings* — find out where you are; *learn the ropes* — learn how a job is done.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To learn something through a painful or unpleasant personal experience, instead of by being told or taught.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often in stories about your own mistakes, followed by a *that* clause or *not to* + verb. *Find out the hard way* is a common variant. *Do something the hard way* is different: it means choosing a difficult method.
entries.pattern: learn (something) the hard way / learn the hard way that … / not to …
examples: I **learned the hard way** that you should always back up your files.
She **learned the hard way** not to lend money to her cousin.
Many first-time homeowners **learn the hard way** that cheap repairs end up costing more.

drill.sentence: After getting a $200 parking ticket, I {{learned the hard way}} that you can't park on that street on Tuesdays.
drill.hint: discovered through a painful experience (not *found out*)

entries.related: *learn your lesson* — understand your mistake and not repeat it; *once bitten, twice shy* — careful after a bad experience; *trial and error* — learning by trying and failing.
